title: Mother Bats’ Hearts Quicken When They Hear Baby’s Cries - Nautilus
gist: A Frontiers in Ethology study found Japanese house bat mothers show heart-rate increases of up to 70 bpm when hearing their own pups' isolation calls, a parallel to human maternal responses.

insights.claim: Japanese house bat mothers reacted exclusively to the recorded isolation calls of their own pups, with heart rate rising by as much as 70 beats per minute.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Shows individual vocal recognition with a measurable physiological response.
insights.locator: The results showed that a bat mother reacted exclusively

insights.claim: The study used four pregnant bats, each with a litter of three pups, and recorded calls at two days old and at 30 days old when pups had transitioned to echolocation calls.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.locator: The study started with four pregnant bats

insights.claim: Mothers responded even more strongly to the echolocation calls of mature offspring than to infant calls, possibly because she knew the pup's sounds better.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Suggests recognition keeps adapting as pups' calls change daily.

insights.claim: Mothers also showed a heart-rate response to calls of unfamiliar adult males, but researchers could not tell whether it was positive arousal or threat perception.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Indicates added complexity in bat social behavior; unresolved.
